name: Wendy Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, government or AI sellers, and your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy Gupta. At 43 I’m junior on a power line crew, though I came in with a vocational certificate. I drive to the electricity company yard before my children wake, put the cones and cable gear on the truck, and help the senior hand repair damaged lines. My partner Luis gets the two children to school when my shift starts early. I still need somebody to check my sequence before I climb, but I like that a repaired street lights up by supper.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a working week manageable at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The mortgage gets paid from a well-paid shift job, and we have more than six months of expenses saved. There are several other electricity companies within reach, though I’m not eager to introduce myself as a beginner all over again. I don’t use AI tools; I keep the laminated procedure card in my pocket. I’d rather learn a step from someone whose hands have done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we can stop talking as though every new app is a revolution. The crew will still set the barriers and repair the line. If the office finishes a few reports faster, good for them; I’ll take a cleaner work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I like knowing the job I’m learning will still be there. The high pay and our savings keep the mortgage comfortable, but I haven’t yet proved I can run a tricky repair without help. I do not want a digital mistake added to that learning curve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d turn up for the same morning truck checks and keep asking the senior hand to review my isolation steps. In the first year I’d carry on logging each repair in my paper notebook. I would not download an AI assistant just because a report takes less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can picture next Tuesday clearly, and the household bills are covered. My nerves are about getting the trade right, not about this small change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the label on a job is unclear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last time a cable label was smeared, I stopped and called the senior hand over. We read the drawing together before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis and I would keep the mortgage standing order and the children’s school routine. The emergency account stays where it is, because nothing in this picture calls for a new purchase.

say: I would tell the crew that **line repairs** still need people and careful barriers.
I would welcome a **cleaner work order** if the office produces one.
think: I feel relief that the **trade I am learning** still looks useful.
Our **mortgage and savings** are manageable, although I still need help on difficult repairs.
do: Continue **truck checks** and ask the senior hand to review isolation steps.
Record each **repair** in my paper notebook during the first year.
feel: Calm about technology, while still careful about **craft mistakes**.
S0.quote: I would not download an AI assistant just because a report takes less time.
fieldNote: Wendy draws confidence from **well-paid shifts** and a strong reserve, without claiming mastery of a trade she is still learning.
She keeps a **paper notebook** and laminated card, and sees no reason to adopt an AI tool under a mild scenario.

steps.text: Continue truck checks and paper repair notes on regular shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the yard to check the route first. An office schedule is only a suggestion until the crew sees the pole and the road. The software may clear desks faster, but nobody should promise a repair by a time chosen from a map. I’m not against a useful timetable; I want a person able to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect planners and dispatchers face the first cuts, and then management may ask us to cover their mistakes with longer days. My job is mostly hands-on, so I expect my wages to continue, though the overtime could change. I’d prefer an ordinary explanation from our supervisor to a glossy screen demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the supervisor at Monday’s briefing whether the new work orders can be changed by the crew. I’d keep a dated list of jobs where access or weather makes the computer time wrong, then share it at the monthly safety meeting. In the first year I’d continue normal callouts while others test the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There is work for me, but I can see a tighter rota putting pressure on the people already learning. The children need my start and finish times to be halfway reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in your dated list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the actual gate number and the time we waited for access. Without that detail, a complaint sounds like somebody wanting a slower day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would less overtime affect home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If overtime fell, the mortgage would still be covered from regular pay. We would skip the extra weekend trip, not change schools or sell the house.

say: I would ask for **crew correction** of computer work orders.
I would remind colleagues that a map cannot set a reliable **repair deadline** by itself.
think: I expect **dispatch roles** to shrink before my hands-on job does.
Our regular pay covers the **mortgage**, though a smaller overtime line would affect weekend spending.
do: Ask the supervisor whether crews can **edit work orders** at Monday’s briefing.
Record bad **time estimates** and share the list at the monthly safety meeting.
Continue normal **callouts** while colleagues test the scheduling software.
feel: Uneasy about a **tighter rota** and uncertain finish times at home.
S1.quote: An office schedule is only a suggestion until the crew sees the pole and the road.
fieldNote: Her public test is whether a **crew can correct** the schedule, rather than whether the software seems modern.
She anticipates less **overtime**, yet says regular pay and savings would cover the mortgage and children’s routine.

steps.text: Continue normal repair callouts under the new schedule
Skip an extra weekend trip if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office and the field are on different clocks. Thinking AI arrives in 2028, and robots capable of our hands-on repairs are around 2031. I’d want the company to tell us what it is actually buying, rather than blur those dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I would still have line shifts even if the office work changes. By 48, when a machine can repair lines as well as us, I might be the junior worker a crew can spare. We can live from our reserve for a while and there are other local utilities, but I would not call that security forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask for my complete skills record and get the mortgage balance in writing. I’d keep going on paid repairs through 2028 and 2029, adding every job I can safely do to that record. If field crews are reduced in 2031, I’d apply for linework vacancies at the other local utilities and cut the holiday budget while we know the new pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can manage a search, but I hate the idea of finally learning the work just before the posts narrow. I’d rather apply for familiar repair work than gamble on a course nobody has explained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide which firms to approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask Luis to look over the list of nearby utilities with me, and we’d agree how far a daily drive could go. Our children will still be at school in 2031; I wouldn’t ask them to move for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if those firms have no vacancies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If none of the nearby firms is hiring, I’d go to the company training office and ask what paid roles a course actually leads to. I would not sign up for training just to fill a waiting list.

say: I would separate **2028 office change** from repair robots expected around 2031.
I would ask the electricity company for a **specific equipment plan** before staffing decisions.
think: I expect **paid line shifts** in the gap, but my junior place could go when capable robots arrive.
Our **savings** offer search time, while nearby jobs are uncertain if every company changes together.
do: Request my **skills record** and a written mortgage balance now.
Continue **paid repairs** through 2029 and record completed jobs.
Apply for nearby **linework vacancies** and cut holiday costs if crews shrink in 2031.
feel: Anxious about the **2031 crew list**, but able to plan a local job search.
S2.quote: I might be the junior worker a crew can spare.
fieldNote: Wendy expects **field work to continue** after thinking AI arrives, but sees her junior position as exposed to the later robots.
Her fallback is a **local repair job search** and a smaller holiday, with retraining considered only if tied to paid posts.

steps.text: Apply to nearby utilities for linework if crews shrink
Cut the family holiday budget if 2031 pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that five years lets us ask proper questions. Thinking AI may take office tasks in 2031, while field robots arrive around 2034. I’d ask the supervisor to put the expected number of line crews on paper each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 48 at the first date and 51 at the second. The extra time could make me a dependable lineworker before anyone chooses which posts to keep, though skill alone may not save a job. The children will be older, but we will still be paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stay on the repair truck and ask for more supervised fault-finding this year. Each spring I’d check the local utility vacancy boards and keep my certificate and repair record ready. In 2032 I’d ask to shadow the meter and inspection crew for two shifts if the supervisor agrees, then apply for a posted inspection role before 2034 if its pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with more room to breathe than in the fast picture. A longer warning does not mean I have to love a new machine. It means I can show a hiring manager what I can really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you whether inspection work suits you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to shadow a real crew, not sit through a sales film. If I find I dislike inspection work, I can still look at the other electricity companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings to stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep our mortgage transfer as it is. We have the reserve to pay for a slower month, but I wouldn’t call it a reason to stop earning.

say: I would ask for **yearly crew numbers** before 2034 field robots arrive.
I would distinguish **2031 office change** from the later effect on line repairs.
think: Five years may give me **better repair skills**, but it cannot promise a retained job.
The **mortgage** still matters even after the children need less school care.
do: Take more **supervised fault-finding** while continuing paid truck shifts.
Check **local vacancies** each spring and keep my repair record ready.
Shadow an **inspection crew** in 2032 if allowed, then apply for a paid vacancy before 2034.
feel: Uneasy, yet able to **show real work** to another employer before the field change.
S3.quote: A longer warning does not mean I have to love a new machine.
fieldNote: She uses the extra years to build **field competence** and test a nearby inspection role, without suddenly becoming an early technology adopter.
The strong reserve is a **bridge for slower months**, not a substitute for continued earnings or a reason to leave work.

steps.text: Continue paid repairs and supervised fault finding
Apply for a posted inspection role if its pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is enough to plan with actual numbers rather than yard rumours. Thinking AI comes in 2036, when I’m 53, and repair robots around 2039, when I’m 56. I’d still want a proper person supervising a line isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be adults by then, so I won’t have school pickups or their childhood costs on the same scale. I might be ready for fewer callouts at 56, but I don’t know what our retirement income will be. A mortgage that is smaller is not a mortgage that has disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a retirement statement and compare it with the mortgage schedule with Luis. I’d keep earning on the line for the next several years and review the local job boards each spring. In 2037 I’d seek a daytime inspection vacancy if one is posted; by 2039 I’d decide on fewer callouts only after seeing our pay and actual retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the next few years. A decade gives me time to finish learning the trade and see what roles truly remain. I would be uneasy if the company refused to show staffing figures later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What matters in the retirement statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the monthly retirement amount, not the age printed on a leaflet. I have seen colleagues assume the payment would match their last wage and get a rude surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change houses in advance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis and I would keep the emergency money for emergencies. We could choose a smaller house later if we wanted, but I’m not making that decision because of a robot date on a card.

say: I would ask for **staffing figures** before the 2039 field change.
I would keep **line isolation** under a named person’s responsibility.
think: Our grown children mean **lower care demands**, but I cannot assume a pension replaces my wage.
I may prefer fewer **callouts at 56** if real income figures support it.
do: Request a **retirement statement** and compare it with our mortgage now.
Continue **paid linework** and check local vacancies each spring.
Seek a posted **daytime inspection job** in 2037 if the pay meets our bills.
feel: Mostly calm with a decade to learn, though future **staffing secrecy** would unsettle me.
S4.quote: A mortgage that is smaller is not a mortgage that has disappeared.
fieldNote: She resists an easy retirement story, asking for a **monthly income figure** before reducing calls at 56.
Her decade plan preserves **paid linework** and leaves the children’s grown-up needs separate from current school costs.

steps.text: Continue paid linework through the long transition
Seek a daytime inspection vacancy in 2037 if pay works

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I’d still be finding my feet when staffing decisions begin, and the repair robots would follow around 2031. A written crew plan and the chance to apply for real local vacancies would help more than an inspirational talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the crew can refuse a job order that leaves too little time for testing. The person who signs the isolation should have room to stop. I would rather explain a late repair than a hurt colleague.

headlineQuote: I would rather explain a late repair than a hurt colleague.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate, high shift pay, a mortgage and two school-age children.
Her household has **strong savings** and several nearby utilities, yet she dislikes risking a new employer while still learning.
She relies on **paper procedures** and senior hands and has never used AI tools in her work.
Across the scenarios she keeps **paid repair work** central, records skills and considers local inspection posts before field robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** concerns her most because robot staffing decisions could come while she is still establishing herself on a crew.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan** and access to real local vacancies would help her choose before repair posts shrink.
